commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether a pre-deployment review of AI-triggered actions and follow-up capacity prevents inequitable effects, and no supplied study documents the hazard. Four sources endorse the practice, one framework and three commentaries, so adoption rests on expert judgment rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The four endorsements come from a framework and three commentaries, which GRADE treats as expert opinion. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence until a comparative study measures equity outcomes with and without the assessment.

The HEAAL framework reports that a workflow double-booking patients predicted to miss appointments was judged to worsen inequities, and one commentary calls for mapping exclusion risks in low-resource maternal and child health settings. These statements describe a concern, but no supplied study measures who was harmed or whether a prior assessment would have changed the result.

One commentary recommends that risk thresholds be co-designed to match service capacity and reviewed as capacity changes, and that evaluation track workload and referral churn. No supplied study reports the staff time, cost, or feasibility of conducting such capacity reviews before deployment, so resource planning has no empirical benchmark.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare deployments with and without a structured pre-deployment review of triggered actions and follow-up capacity, measuring outcomes such as missed follow-up, appointment access, and referral completion by payer, language, and literacy group. A first step would be observational documentation of how often prediction-triggered workflows, such as double-booking or referrals without staffed follow-up, produce differential access.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The endorsements focus on these groups conceptually, yet health systems serving them have no outcome data showing whether the assessment reduces harm.
